mainTopic: The two evils of עבודה זרה, why שמואל aged early, and רב נחמן's meal with רבי יצחק ending in the parable of the tree
overview: This amud opens by finishing רבי יצחק's answer to רב נחמן. The 'two evils' in ירמיה are one sin, עבודה זרה, which is as bad as two. A ברייתא adds that even nations who worship fire and water never swap their gods, yet Israel left the true God. Next, רב נחמן asks how the verse can call שמואל 'old' when he died at fifty-two. רבי יצחק answers in the name of רבי יוחנן that God made old age come on him early. שמואל had prayed that שאול's reign not end in his lifetime, and דוד's reign could not be delayed. So שמואל had to die first, and looking old kept people from gossiping that he died young for a sin. The גמרא proves that one person's life can give way to another's. Then, at a meal, רבי יצחק will not talk while eating. Afterward he teaches that יעקב אבינו did not die, and that saying רחב's name arouses those who knew her. As they part, he blesses רב נחמן with the parable of a perfect tree whose saplings should be like it, a blessing that ends on the next amud.

steps.title: The one sin that counts as two is idol worship
steps.stepSummary: רבי יצחק finishes his answer. The 'two evils' of the verse are one sin, עבודה זרה, which weighs as much as two sins.
steps.simpleTranslation: [It is one sin that] is equal to two. And what is it? Idol worship, as it says: 'For My people have done two evils: they left Me, the source of living water, to dig for themselves cisterns, broken cisterns.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is finishing רבי יצחק's answer on the previous amud. The verse's 'two evils' are really one sin, עבודה זרה, which is as serious as two.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The verse says 'two evils,' but it seems to describe one act: leaving God for something else. רבי יצחק explains that the act is עבודה זרה, and it is so serious that it counts double. In one move a person leaves the living spring and also chases broken, useless cisterns.

keyTerms.meaning: the source of living (flowing) water, meaning God

steps.confusionAlert: This amud starts in the middle of a sentence. The first words, 'equal to two,' finish רבי יצחק's answer earlier. They are not a new statement.

phrases.english: [one sin that] is equal to two.
And what is it? Idol worship,
as it is written: 'For My people have committed two evils:
they have forsaken Me, the fountain of living waters,
to hew for themselves cisterns, broken cisterns.'

steps.triggerLanguage: שקולה כשתים, ומאי ניהו — עבודה זרה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes רבי יצחק's answer to רב נחמן's question (earlier) about the 'two evils.'
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The 'two evils' are one sin, עבודה זרה, which is as severe as two.

steps.title: A second verse shows the sin is swapping God for idols
steps.stepSummary: Another verse in the same chapter shows the sin is trading God for false gods, something even the pagan nations never did.
steps.simpleTranslation: And it says about them: 'Cross over to the islands of Kittim and look, send to Kedar and check carefully... Has any nation ever swapped its gods, even though they are not real gods? But My people swapped its Glory for something useless.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a nearby verse to prove that the sin being described is עבודה זרה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first verse only says the people 'left' God. This second verse names the sin outright: they 'swapped' their Glory (God) for something useless. It also stresses how shocking this is, since no other nation ever swaps its gods, even though those gods are fake.

keyTerms.meaning: the islands of Kittim (a far-off western people)
for something that does not help (useless)

phrases.english: And it is written about them:
'For cross over to the isles of the Kittim and see,
and send to Kedar and observe carefully, etc.
phrases.notes: 'etc.' leaves out: 'and see if there has been such a thing'

phrases.aramaic: הַהֵימִיר גּוֹי אֱלֹהִים וְהֵמָּה לֹא אֱלֹהִים
phrases.english: Has a nation exchanged its gods, though they are no gods?
But My people has exchanged its Glory for what does not profit.'

steps.triggerLanguage: וכתיב בהו
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports step 1's claim that the 'two evils' refers to עבודה זרה.
steps.raayaObject: That the sin in the 'two evils' verse is עבודה זרה.
steps.raayaSupportSource: ירמיה 2:10–11, which describes Israel 'swapping its Glory' for something useless.

steps.title: A teaching explains the verse: fire-worshippers and water-worshippers kept their gods
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא explains the verse. The Kittites serve fire and Kedar serves water. Even though they know water puts out fire, neither nation switched gods, yet Israel did.
steps.simpleTranslation: It was taught: the Kittites worship fire, and the people of Kedar worship water. Even though they know that water puts out fire, they did not switch their gods. 'But My people swapped its Glory for something useless.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes a ברייתא that explains why the verse mentions Kittim and Kedar in particular.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The fire-worshippers could see that their god loses to water, and still they stayed loyal to it. This makes Israel's betrayal look even worse. Israel left the one true God, who never fails, for idols that really are useless.
steps.confusionAlert: Here כותיים does NOT mean the Samaritans (כותים). It means the people of כתים from the verse.
steps.whatToRemember: עבודה זרה is so serious it counts as two sins. Israel's betrayal is shocking because even pagans whose gods visibly fail never switch gods.

phrases.english: It was taught: The Kittites worship fire,
and the people of Kedar worship water,

phrases.aramaic: וְאַף עַל פִּי שֶׁיּוֹדְעִים שֶׁהַמַּיִם מְכַבִּין אֶת הָאֵשׁ —
phrases.english: and even though they know that water extinguishes fire,
they did not exchange their gods;
'But My people has exchanged its Glory for what does not profit.'

steps.triggerLanguage: תנא: כותיים עובדים לאש
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains the verse from step 2, showing why Kittim and Kedar are mentioned.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The nations stay loyal to gods that visibly fail, while Israel left the true God. This shows how great the sin of עבודה זרה is.

steps.title: רב נחמן asks what 'when שמואל was old' means
steps.stepSummary: רב נחמן asks רבי יצחק a new question about the verse 'And it was when שמואל grew old.'
steps.simpleTranslation: And רב נחמן said to רבי יצחק: What does the verse mean, 'And it was when שמואל was old'?
steps.whatsHappening: רב נחמן opens a new topic by asking רבי יצחק to explain a verse about שמואל. This is a setup line, and the next step spells out what is bothering him.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is the same pair of rabbis as before, now moving to a new verse. On its own the question sounds simple. The real problem appears in the next line.

keyTerms.meaning: what is the meaning of what is written

phrases.aramaic: וַאֲמַר לֵיהּ רַב נַחְמָן לְרַבִּי יִצְחָק,
phrases.english: And Rav Naḥman said to Rabbi Yitzḥak:
What is the meaning of that which is written: 'And it came to pass when Samuel was old'?

steps.triggerLanguage: ואמר ליה רב נחמן לרבי יצחק, מאי דכתיב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic between the same two rabbis.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What does the verse mean when it calls שמואל 'old'?

steps.title: שמואל died at only fifty-two, so how was he 'old'?
steps.stepSummary: רב נחמן explains his difficulty. שמואל died at fifty-two, as a ברייתא says, so he was never really old.
steps.simpleTranslation: Did שמואל really get that old? He was only fifty-two! As the Master said: one who dies at fifty-two, that is the death of שמואל from Ramah.
steps.whatsHappening: רב נחמן shows why the verse is hard. He brings a ברייתא proving that שמואל died at just fifty-two.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Fifty-two is not old age, yet the verse says שמואל 'was old.' The ברייתא (which deals with the age of a כרת death) uses שמואל's death at fifty-two as an example. So the verse seems to clash with the known facts.

keyTerms.meaning: as the Master said (citing a teaching)

phrases.english: And did Samuel really grow so old?
But he was only fifty-two years old,

phrases.aramaic: דְּאָמַר מָר: מֵת בַּחֲמִישִּׁים וּשְׁתַּיִם שָׁנָה,
phrases.english: as the Master said: One who died at fifty-two years,
phrases.notes: From a ברייתא about the age of a כרת death

phrases.english: this is the death of Samuel of Ramah.

steps.triggerLanguage: ומי סיב שמואל כולי האי? והא בר חמישים ושתים הוה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains what is difficult about the verse in step 4.
steps.kashyaTarget: The verse's description of שמואל as 'old' (שמואל א 8:1).
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A ברייתא teaches that שמואל died at fifty-two, which is not old age, so how could the verse call him old?

steps.title: Old age came upon שמואל early
steps.stepSummary: רבי יצחק answers in the name of רבי יוחנן: old age 'jumped' on שמואל before his time. This is linked to God's regret over making שאול king.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: This is what רבי יוחנן said: Old age jumped onto him early, as it says: 'I regret that I made שאול king.'
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יצחק answers that שמואל really did become old, but early and suddenly, long before the normal age.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both facts are true: שמואל was young in years but old in body. The verse 'I regret that I made שאול king' hints at the cause. God's decision to remove שאול led to שמואל aging early, as the next step explains.

keyTerms.meaning: old age jumped onto him (came suddenly and early)

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ, הָכִי אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן:
phrases.english: He said to him: Thus said Rabbi Yoḥanan:
Old age sprang upon him,
as it is written: 'I regret that I made Saul king.'

steps.triggerLanguage: אמר ליה, הכי אמר רבי יוחנן: זקנה קפצה עליו
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the difficulty in step 5.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reconciliation: both facts are true. He was young in years but aged suddenly.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: 'Old' must mean old in years, which clashes with dying at fifty-two.
steps.terutzMaskana: שמואל aged suddenly and early, connected to God's regret over making שאול king.

steps.title: שמואל prays that his life's work not be undone while he lives
steps.stepSummary: שמואל pleads with God: You compared me to משה and אהרן, whose work was never undone in their lifetimes, so do not undo my work (anointing שאול) while I am alive.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said before Him: Master of the World! You counted me as equal to משה and אהרן, as it says: 'משה and אהרן among His priests, and שמואל among those who call His Name.' Just as משה and אהרן did not see their work undone while they lived, so too let my work not be undone while I live.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tells of שמואל's prayer after God regretted making שאול king. This prayer sets up the explanation, which continues next, of why שמואל aged early.
steps.deeperAnalysis: שמואל anointed שאול, so ending שאול's reign would undo שמואל's work. He argues from a verse that groups him with משה and אהרן, whose work stood firm during their lives. Because of this plea, שאול's reign cannot end while שמואל lives. So שמואל must die first, and the next steps explain why God made him look old.

phrases.english: He said before Him: Master of the Universe!
You considered me equal to Moses and Aaron,
as it is written: 'Moses and Aaron among His priests,
and Samuel among those who call upon His Name.'

phrases.aramaic: מָה מֹשֶׁה וְאַהֲרֹן לֹא בָּטְלוּ מַעֲשֵׂה יְדֵיהֶם בְּחַיֵּיהֶם,
phrases.english: Just as Moses and Aaron, their handiwork was not annulled in their lifetimes,

phrases.aramaic: אַף אֲנִי לֹא יִתְבַּטֵּל מַעֲשֵׂה יָדַי בְּחַיַּי.
phrases.english: so too, let my handiwork not be annulled in my lifetime.

steps.triggerLanguage: אמר לפניו: רבונו של עולם! שקלתני כמשה ואהרן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Expands on רבי יוחנן's answer by telling what שמואל said after God's regret over שאול.
steps.whyThisMatters: This plea is what explains early aging. It shows how God honored שמואל's request, and the explanation finishes next.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: שמואל asked, like משה and אהרן, not to see his life's work (שאול's kingship) undone in his lifetime.

steps.title: God's dilemma: three options, each with a problem
steps.stepSummary: הקב"ה weighs three options: letting שאול die, letting שמואל die young, or letting neither die. Each option has a problem.
steps.simpleTranslation: הקב"ה said: What should I do? If שאול dies now, שמואל will not allow it. If שמואל dies young, people will gossip about him. If neither dies, there is another problem: the time for דוד's kingdom has already come, and one kingdom may not overlap with the next even by a hair's width.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא shows God thinking through His options after שמואל's plea in the last step. This sets up God's solution in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: שמואל had begged that שאול not lose the kingship during his lifetime. If שמואל simply died young, people would think he had sinned. Waiting is also impossible, because דוד's reign has a fixed start time that cannot be delayed.

keyTerms.meaning: one kingdom does not touch (overlap with) another

steps.whyThisMatters: The principle that one kingdom cannot cut into another's time leads to the question in step 11: can one person's life really give way to another's? Step 12 answers yes.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא: הֵיכִי אֶעֱבֵיד?
phrases.english: The Holy One, Blessed be He, said: What shall I do?

phrases.aramaic: לֵימוּת שָׁאוּל — לָא קָא שָׁבֵיק שְׁמוּאֵל,
phrases.english: Should Saul die? Samuel will not allow it.
phrases.notes: שמואל prayed that his work not be undone in his lifetime.

phrases.english: Should Samuel die while young? People will murmur about him.
phrases.notes: They would think he died early because of a sin.

phrases.aramaic: לָא לֵימוּת שָׁאוּל וְלָא לֵימוּת שְׁמוּאֵל —
phrases.english: Should neither Saul nor Samuel die?
The kingdom of David has already arrived,
and one kingdom does not touch its fellow kingdom
even by a hair's breadth.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא: הֵיכִי אֶעֱבֵיד
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Responds to שמואל's plea in step 7 by laying out God's dilemma.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Every simple option fails: שאול cannot die, שמואל cannot die young without gossip, and דוד's reign cannot be delayed.

steps.title: God's solution: make שמואל old early
steps.stepSummary: הקב"ה decides to bring old age suddenly on שמואל, so that his death will not seem early.
steps.simpleTranslation: הקב"ה said: I will make old age jump upon him.
steps.whatsHappening: God picks the solution. שמואל will look old, so when he dies people will not gossip.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This connects back to step 6, which said old age 'jumped' on שמואל. It also answers רב נחמן's question from step 5 about how שמואל could be called old when he died at fifty-two. He was old in appearance, though not in years.
steps.whatToRemember: שמואל died at fifty-two but looked old, because God made old age come early. This solved the dilemma without gossip and without delaying דוד.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא: אַקְפִּיץ עָלָיו זִקְנָה.
phrases.english: The Holy One, Blessed be He, said: I will spring old age upon him.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא: אַקְפִּיץ עָלָיו זִקְנָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Resolves the three-way dilemma of step 8.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: Early old age let שמואל die without suspicion of sin, and דוד's kingdom came on time.

steps.title: Support from the verse about Gibeah and Ramah
steps.stepSummary: A verse places שאול in both גבעה and רמה. The גמרא reads this as hinting that שמואל of רמה's prayer kept שאול reigning in גבעה.
steps.simpleTranslation: This is what the verse means: 'And שאול was sitting in גבעה under the tamarisk tree in רמה.' But what does גבעה have to do with רמה? They are two different places! Rather, the verse is teaching you: Who caused שאול to sit as king in גבעה for two and a half years? The prayer of שמואל from רמה.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a verse to back up the story. The verse seems to mix up two places.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The odd wording, putting שאול 'in גבעה' and 'in רמה' at once, becomes a hint. שאול's extra time on the throne came from the prayer of שמואל, who was from רמה. This supports step 7, where שמואל prayed that שאול's kingship not end in his lifetime.

keyTerms.meaning: what does one have to do with the other?
rather, it comes to tell you

phrases.english: This is what is written: 'And Saul was sitting in Gibeah
under the tamarisk tree in Ramah' (I Samuel 22:6).

phrases.aramaic: וְכִי מָה עִנְיַן גִּבְעָה אֵצֶל רָמָה?
phrases.english: But what does Gibeah have to do with Ramah?
Rather, it is to tell you:
Who caused Saul to sit in Gibeah
for two and a half years?
The prayer of Samuel of Ramah.

steps.triggerLanguage: הַיְינוּ דִּכְתִיב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings a verse supporting the story of שמואל's prayer and its effect.
steps.raayaObject: That שמואל's prayer kept שאול reigning during שמואל's lifetime.
steps.raayaSupportSource: שמואל א 22:6, which puts שאול in both גבעה and רמה.

steps.title: Can one person really be pushed aside for another?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the story: can שמואל's life really be cut short just because דוד's time has come?
steps.simpleTranslation: And is one man really pushed aside because of another man?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on the story. It seems unfair that שמואל should die early only because it is time for דוד to reign.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 8 assumed that דוד's reign could not be delayed, even if this meant שמואל had to die. The question asks whether a righteous person's life can be shortened for someone else's sake, and not because of his own deeds.

keyTerms.meaning: a man before (because of) another man

phrases.english: And is a man pushed aside before another man?

steps.triggerLanguage: וּמִי מִידְּחֵי גַּבְרָא מִקַּמֵּי גַּבְרָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the assumption behind step 8 that שמואל's life had to give way to דוד's reign.
steps.kashyaTarget: The idea that שמואל's lifespan was shortened because דוד's kingdom had arrived.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: It seems unlikely that a person's life is cut short for another person's sake and not because of his own actions.

steps.title: Yes: proof from 'by the words of My mouth'
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers yes, from a verse in הושע. God says He killed the prophets 'by the words of My mouth,' meaning by His decree and not because of their deeds.
steps.simpleTranslation: Yes. As רבי שמואל בר נחמני said in the name of רבי יוחנן: What does the verse mean, 'Therefore I have cut down through the prophets; I have killed them by the words of My mouth'? It does not say 'by their deeds' but 'by the words of My mouth.' So we see that one man can be pushed aside for another.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge with a clear yes, and proves it from a verse.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The proof comes from the exact wording. The verse could have said the prophets died 'because of their deeds.' Instead it says 'by the words of My mouth,' meaning by God's decree alone. So a person can die for reasons that have nothing to do with his own sins, like making way for the next era.

keyTerms.meaning: by the words of My mouth

steps.whatToRemember: A person's life can end through God's decree, for example to make room for another leader's era, and not only because of his own deeds.
steps.confusionAlert: Do not read this as saying שמואל did something wrong. The whole point is the opposite: his early death was not caused by his deeds.

phrases.aramaic: אִין, דְּאָמַר רַבִּי שְׁמוּאֵל בַּר נַחְמָנִי אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן:
phrases.english: Yes, as Rabbi Shmuel bar Naḥmani said that Rabbi Yoḥanan said:
What is the meaning of what is written:
'Therefore I have hewn by the prophets,
I have slain them by the words of My mouth' (Hosea 6:5)?
'By their deeds' is not stated,
but rather 'by the words of My mouth.'
Apparently, a man is pushed aside before another man.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִין, דְּאָמַר רַבִּי שְׁמוּאֵל בַּר נַחְמָנִי אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 11 by accepting its premise as true and proving it.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Accepts the challenged premise and proves it from a verse.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: A person dies only because of his own deeds, so שמואל's early death would need a sin to explain it.
steps.terutzMaskana: God can end a life by decree alone, so שמואל's life could give way to דוד's era.

steps.title: At a meal, רב נחמן asks for a Torah thought
steps.stepSummary: A new story begins. רב נחמן and רבי יצחק are eating together, and רב נחמן asks רבי יצחק to say something of Torah.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב נחמן and רבי יצחק were sitting at a meal. רב נחמן said to רבי יצחק: Let the master say something.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens a new story between the same two Sages who discussed the earlier questions. This sets up רבי יצחק's reply.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is the start of a new section, connected to the earlier one only by the same pair of Sages. רב נחמן asks for a דבר תורה, and the reply comes in the next step.

keyTerms.meaning: let the master say a matter (a Torah thought)

phrases.english: Rav Naḥman and Rabbi Yitzḥak
were sitting at a meal.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רַב נַחְמָן לְרַבִּי יִצְחָק:
phrases.english: Rav Naḥman said to Rabbi Yitzḥak:
Let the master say a matter.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַב נַחְמָן וְרַבִּי יִצְחָק הֲווֹ יָתְבִי בִּסְעוּדְתָּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new story with the same two Sages as steps 4–12.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: A Torah teaching from רבי יצחק during the meal.

steps.title: No talking during a meal, because of the danger of choking
steps.stepSummary: רבי יצחק declines, quoting רבי יוחנן: one should not talk while eating, because food might go down the windpipe.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: This is what רבי יוחנן said: We do not talk during a meal, because the windpipe might open before the food pipe, and the person could come into danger.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יצחק answers that he will not talk now. His reason is a teaching of רבי יוחנן.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Talking opens the windpipe (קנה). If food goes there instead of into the food pipe (ושט), a person can choke. So even Torah talk waits until after eating, which is why רבי יצחק turns down the request for now.
steps.whyThisMatters: This is the source for the practice of not talking while eating, out of concern for choking.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ, הָכִי אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן:
phrases.english: He said to him: So said Rabbi Yoḥanan:
One may not converse during a meal,
lest the windpipe come before the food pipe
and he come to danger.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ, הָכִי אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן: אֵין מְסִיחִין בִּסְעוּדָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Responds to רב נחמן's request in step 13.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: רבי יצחק refuses to speak during the meal, citing רבי יוחנן's rule that talking while eating risks choking.

steps.title: After the meal: יעקב אבינו did not die
steps.stepSummary: Now that the meal is over, רבי יצחק shares a teaching from רבי יוחנן: יעקב אבינו did not die.
steps.simpleTranslation: After they ate, he said to him: This is what רבי יוחנן said: Our father יעקב did not die.
steps.whatsHappening: The meal is over, so רבי יצחק is now willing to share Torah. He quotes a surprising statement from רבי יוחנן: יעקב אבינו did not die.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This finishes the setup from Step 14. רבי יצחק would not speak while eating, but now that they are done he is free to talk. The claim is startling, and it sets up the challenge that comes next.

phrases.english: After they had eaten, he said to him:
phrases.notes: רבי יצחק is speaking to רב נחמן, now that the meal is finished.

phrases.english: This is what Rabbi Yochanan said:
Our father Jacob did not die.

steps.triggerLanguage: בָּתַר דִּסְעוּד אֲמַר לֵיהּ, הָכִי אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Carries out the request from Step 13, now that the reason for holding back in Step 14 (eating) no longer applies.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: In the name of רבי יוחנן: יעקב אבינו did not die.

steps.title: But he was eulogized, embalmed and buried
steps.stepSummary: רב נחמן challenges the claim. The Torah describes יעקב being eulogized, embalmed, and buried, so how can anyone say he did not die?
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: Was it for nothing that the eulogizers eulogized him, the embalmers embalmed him, and the buriers buried him?
steps.whatsHappening: רב נחמן attacks the statement. The Torah itself tells us about יעקב's funeral, so he must have died.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The challenge comes straight from the פסוקים in בראשית that describe יעקב's הספד, embalming (חניטה), and burial. Those actions only make sense for someone who has died. So the claim seems to contradict the plain story of the Torah.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: וְכִי בִּכְדִי סְפַדוּ סַפְדָּנַיָּא
phrases.english: He said to him: Was it for nothing that the eulogizers eulogized him
and the embalmers embalmed him
and the buriers buried him?

steps.triggerLanguage: וְכִי בִּכְדִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the statement of Step 15.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that יעקב אבינו did not die.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The Torah describes a full funeral, with eulogy, embalming, and burial. That proves he died.

steps.title: The verse links יעקב to his living descendants
steps.stepSummary: רבי יצחק answers that he is reading a פסוק in ירמיהו. That פסוק puts יעקב side by side with his descendants: just as they are alive, so is he.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: I am explaining a verse, as it says: 'And you, do not fear, My servant יעקב, says ה׳, and do not be dismayed, ישראל, for I will save you from afar, and your seed from the land of their captivity.' The verse compares him to his seed. Just as his seed is alive, so too he is alive.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יצחק defends the statement. He says it comes from a פסוק, not from ignoring the funeral story.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק speaks to יעקב and to his descendants (זרעו) together, promising to save both. Because the two are joined (a היקש), whatever is true of the descendants is true of יעקב. The descendants are alive when they are redeemed, so יעקב must also be 'alive.' The answer does not deny that a funeral took place. It explains the claim as a reading of a פסוק.
steps.confusionAlert: רבי יצחק does not deny that the burial happened. He only says the 'did not die' idea comes from a פסוק. רש״י explains it was only to the onlookers that יעקב seemed dead.
steps.whatToRemember: יעקב אבינו לא מת is learned from a פסוק that links יעקב to his living descendants: just as they live, he lives.

phrases.english: He said to him: I am expounding a verse,
as it is said: 'And you, do not fear, My servant Jacob,'
says the Lord, 'and do not be dismayed, Israel,'
'for behold, I will save you from afar,'
'and your seed from the land of their captivity.'
The verse compares him to his seed:
just as his seed is alive,
so too he is alive.

steps.triggerLanguage: מִקְרָא אֲנִי דּוֹרֵשׁ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of Step 16.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The statement seemed to ignore the plain story of יעקב's funeral.
steps.terutzMaskana: The statement is a דרשה. The פסוק links יעקב to his living descendants, so he too is considered alive.

steps.title: Saying רחב's name arouses desire
steps.stepSummary: רבי יצחק makes a new statement. Anyone who says 'רחב, רחב' immediately has a seminal emission, because her beauty was so great.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יצחק said: Anyone who says 'רחב, רחב' immediately has a seminal emission.
steps.whatsHappening: A new topic starts. רבי יצחק makes a strong statement about the power of רחב's beauty: even saying her name twice can arouse desire.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רחב was famous for her beauty (see מגילה טו.). The claim is that her name alone was enough to stir up desire. The statement is said in a very general way ('anyone'), and that sets up the challenge that follows.

keyTerms.meaning: Rahab, the woman of Jericho known for her great beauty

phrases.english: Rabbi Yitzchak said:
Anyone who says 'Rahab, Rahab'
immediately has a seminal emission.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי יִצְחָק: כׇּל הָאוֹמֵר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new, unrelated teaching shared during the same conversation.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Saying 'רחב, רחב' immediately arouses a person to the point of emission.

steps.title: רב נחמן says it does not affect him
steps.stepSummary: רב נחמן pushes back. He says her name himself and nothing happens to him.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב נחמן said to him: I say it, and it does not affect me!
steps.whatsHappening: רב נחמן challenges the statement from his own experience. If it were true of 'anyone,' it would happen to him too.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The attack is aimed at the word 'anyone' (כל) in Step 18. One real person who is not affected is enough to disprove such a sweeping claim.

phrases.english: Rav Nachman said to him:
I say it, and it does not affect me!

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רַב נַחְמָן: אֲנָא אָמֵינָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the broad claim of Step 18.
steps.kashyaTarget: The word 'anyone' (כל האומר) in רבי יצחק's statement.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Here is a case of someone who says the name and is not affected, so the claim cannot apply to everyone.

steps.title: It applies only to someone who knew her
steps.stepSummary: רבי יצחק narrows the claim. It applies only to a man who actually knew רחב and recognized her.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: When I said it, I meant someone who knew her and recognized her.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יצחק answers by limiting his statement. It was never meant for everyone, only for those who had personally met רחב.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The answer works by defining the case more narrowly. Someone who never saw רחב, like רב נחמן, has no memory of her face for the name to stir up. So the challenge goes away.

keyTerms.meaning: When I said it, I meant
Someone who knew her and recognized her

phrases.english: He said to him: When I said it,
I meant someone who knew her and recognized her.

steps.triggerLanguage: כִּי קָאָמֵינָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of Step 19.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The statement seemed to cover every person who says the name.
steps.terutzMaskana: It covers only those who personally knew and recognized רחב.

steps.title: At parting, רב נחמן asks for a blessing
steps.stepSummary: As the two take leave of each other, רב נחמן asks רבי יצחק to bless him.
steps.simpleTranslation: When they were taking leave of one another, he said to him: Let the master bless me!
steps.whatsHappening: The visit is ending, and רב נחמן asks for a ברכה. This sets up רבי יצחק's famous answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Asking a great person for a ברכה when parting is a natural custom. The request opens the last part of the story. רבי יצחק will answer with a משל instead of a simple blessing.

phrases.english: When they were taking leave of one another,
he said to him: Let the master bless me!
phrases.notes: רב נחמן is asking רבי יצחק.

steps.triggerLanguage: כִּי הֲווֹ מִיפַּטְרִי מֵהֲדָדֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves the meal story toward its close, with a request for a ברכה.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: A farewell ברכה from רבי יצחק.

steps.title: The parable of the tree in the desert
steps.stepSummary: רבי יצחק begins a משל. A tired, hungry, thirsty traveler finds a tree with sweet fruit, nice shade, and a stream of water underneath, and he enjoys all three.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: I will tell you a parable. What is this like? A person was walking in the desert, hungry, tired and thirsty. He found a tree with sweet fruit and pleasant shade, and a stream of water flowing beneath it. He ate from its fruit, drank from its water, and sat in its shade.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יצחק answers the request with a story instead of a direct ברכה. This part sets the scene. The point comes in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The tree stands for רב נחמן, and the traveler stands for רבי יצחק, who enjoyed רב נחמן's hospitality. Each good thing the tree offers matches a need the traveler had: fruit for hunger, water for thirst, shade for tiredness. This builds up the question of what blessing could be left to give.

keyTerms.meaning: I will tell you a parable

phrases.english: He said to him: I will tell you a parable.
To what is this comparable?
To a person who was walking in the desert
and he was hungry, tired, and thirsty,
and he found a tree whose fruits were sweet
and whose shade was pleasant,
and a stream of water flowed beneath it.
He ate from its fruits, drank from its water,
and sat in its shade.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶמְשׁוֹל לְךָ מָשָׁל, לְמָה הַדָּבָר דּוֹמֶה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts the answer to the request in Step 21.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: A משל that sets the scene: a tree that already gives everything the traveler needed.

steps.title: What blessing can you give a perfect tree
steps.stepSummary: The traveler wants to bless the tree, but it already has sweet fruit, nice shade, and water. So he blesses it that all the saplings planted from it should be like it. The sentence continues on the next amud.
steps.simpleTranslation: When he wanted to leave, he said: Tree, tree, with what shall I bless you? If I say your fruits should be sweet, your fruits are already sweet. If I say your shade should be pleasant, your shade is already pleasant. If I say a stream should flow beneath you, a stream already flows beneath you. Rather: may it be God's will that all the saplings planted from you...
steps.whatsHappening: This is the heart of the משל. Every normal blessing would only wish the tree what it already has, so the traveler blesses its future saplings instead.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יצחק is hinting that רב נחמן already has everything: Torah, wealth, and even children. Wishing him those things adds nothing. The only meaningful ברכה left is that his offspring, the 'saplings,' should be like him. This passage stops mid-sentence, and the end of the ברכה comes on the next amud.

keyTerms.meaning: With what shall I bless you?

steps.confusionAlert: The sentence is not finished here. The ending of the ברכה (that the saplings should be like the tree) comes on the next amud.
steps.whyThisMatters: This משל is the source for a well-known way of blessing a great person: that their children should be like them.

phrases.english: And when he wished to leave, he said:
Tree, tree, with what shall I bless you?

phrases.aramaic: אִם אוֹמַר לְךָ שֶׁיְּהוּ פֵּירוֹתֶיךָ מְתוּקִין —
phrases.english: If I say to you that your fruits should be sweet,
your fruits are already sweet;

phrases.aramaic: שֶׁיְּהֵא צִילְּךָ נָאֶה — הֲרֵי צִילְּךָ נָאֶה,
phrases.english: that your shade should be pleasant, your shade is already pleasant;
that a stream of water should flow beneath you,
a stream of water already flows beneath you.
Rather: may it be God's will
that all the saplings that are planted from you
phrases.notes: The sentence continues on the next amud.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִילָן אִילָן, בַּמָּה אֲבָרֶכְךָ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues and delivers the point of the משל begun in Step 22.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Since the tree (רב נחמן) already has every good thing, the blessing left is that its saplings (his offspring) should be like it. The full wording continues on the next amud.
